blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) defines substantive offenses and prescribes corresponding penalties across India.
The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) establishes the procedural mechanism for criminal investigations, arrests, trials, and bail.
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 modernizes and replaces the procedural framework of CrPC 1973.
The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (PCA) penalizes bribery, criminal misconduct, and corrupt acts committed by public servants.

blocks.content: The Indian Penal Code, 1860 is the official criminal code of India. It was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which came into force on 1 July 2024. For banking law exams, knowledge of both may be needed.

cells: Acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention
Criminal Conspiracy — agreement between 2+ persons to commit offence
Theft in dwelling house, building, tent, vessel
Theft by clerk or servant of property in master's possession
Robbery and Dacoity — theft/extortion with force/fear; 5+ persons = dacoity
Criminal Breach of Trust — dishonestly misappropriates property entrusted; Section 409 = by public servant/banker/agent
Cheating; Section 420 = cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property; 7 years imprisonment
Forgery; using forged document; counterfeiting; Section 468 = forgery for cheating; Section 471 = using forged document knowing it to be forged
Counterfeiting currency notes; punishment up to life imprisonment (Section 489A)

blocks.content: Important: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 replaces IPC from 1 July 2024. BNS has 358 sections vs IPC's 511. Key addition: organised crime, terrorism as separate chapter in BNS.

rows: Outlines Machinery for investigation, arrest, trial, and appeal

blocks.content: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was replaced by Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) effective 1 July 2024. It governs the procedural aspects of criminal law in India.

cells: Police can arrest without warrant; register FIR without Magistrate's permission (serious crimes)
Police cannot arrest without warrant; need Magistrate's permission to investigate
Information of cognizable offence given to police; right to get free copy; cannot be quashed lightly
Police can arrest in cognizable cases without warrant; must follow procedure; Section 41A: notice before arrest if arrest not immediately necessary
Bailable offences: bail as of right; Non-bailable: court's discretion; Anticipatory bail (Section 438): granted by Sessions Court or HC before arrest
Police report submitted to Magistrate after investigation; within 60/90 days
Summons case: offence punishable with imprisonment less than 2 years; Warrant case: 2 years or more
Quick disposal of petty offences; imprisonment not more than 3 months; Magistrate must state reasons
Mutually satisfactory disposition; for offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment; not for socioeconomic offences or offences against women/children
Settlement between parties for certain offences; list in Section 320; some require court permission

items: Differentiate substantive law (IPC/BNS) from procedural law (CrPC/BNSS) as questions frequently test this fundamental distinction.
Memorize the enactment years and key modern replacement statutes (BNS 2023 replacing IPC 1860 and BNSS 2023 replacing CrPC 1973).
Focus on the legal definition of 'public servant' and required sanction for prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

cells: Public servants including bank employees (nationalised and private banks are 'public servants' under PCA for certain purposes)
Section 7: Public servant taking bribe; Section 8: Bribe giver (abettor); Section 11: Public servant obtaining undue advantage without consideration
Section 13(1)(e): Possession of assets disproportionate to known income sources; reverse burden of proof
Section 7: 3–7 years imprisonment + fine; Section 13: 4–10 years + fine
Section 19: Prosecution of public servant requires prior sanction of appropriate Government (employer)
Section 3: Special Judges appointed to try PCA offences; fast-track
Bribe giver also criminal; no immunity except immediate reporting to law enforcement; protection for reporting bribery promptly
Superintendence of CBI in anti-corruption matters; investigates complaints against Grade-A officers
Investigates PCA offences by Central Government employees; needs consent of State for State Government employees (except in some HC-directed cases)
